cultivar: Bai Ye (Lingtou Dancong cultivar, a Fenghuang Shui Xian selection)
processing: Sun-withered, shaken overnight to a medium-light oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted, usually to a medium level that deepens its honey note.
harvest_season: Spring, from late March in the low gardens to late April higher up; the earliest-sprouting dancong, with autumn and winter pickings common in the lowlands.
appearance_dry: Long, slightly loose olive-brown strips with a yellowish tint and a sweet honey smell.
appearance_wet: Long, pale yellow-green leaves with red edges, visibly lighter in colour than other dancong.
taste_profile: Honey and a soft orchid note, a light-to-medium body, a gentle roasted sweetness and a short, clean finish; pleasant and simple.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. It is forgiving and makes a good pot tea too: 4 g per 200 ml for a minute, three times. Not a tea to stretch past seven steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, often without a season because the lowland gardens pick several times; spring tea is on sale from May. Lightly roasted lots are best within a year, medium roasts keep two years sealed and dry; it is not aged.
description:
Bai Ye, white leaf, is the dancong that pays the bills: an early, hardy, high-yielding strain with pale leaves and a straightforward honey-and-orchid cup, planted all over the Fenghuang range and the neighbouring county of Raoping. A great deal of inexpensive tea labelled Mi Lan Xiang or simply Phoenix oolong is Bai Ye.

The strain is usually identified with the plant selected at Lingtou village in Raoping and registered as the national cultivar Lingtou Dancong, with the name depending on where it grew: Lingtou Dancong in Raoping, Bai Ye in the Fenghuang gardens. Some Chaozhou sellers treat them as separate strains. Its pale yellow-green foliage gives it the name, it sprouts early, and it crops reliably, which is why farmers love it and why connoisseurs tend to look down on it.

It is made like other dancong, withered, shaken overnight, rolled into strips and charcoal roasted, and makers usually give it a medium roast, since its honey note deepens with fire and its florals are not delicate enough to protect. In the cup it is honeyed and lightly floral, with a soft body, a toasty sweetness and a short, clean finish, without the long cooling aftertaste of the high-mountain strains.

Brew it with the standard dancong technique and it will give seven decent steeps; brew it in a pot and it will give a pleasant everyday oolong. It does not punish mistakes the way Ya Shi Xiang does, which makes it a good tea to practise Chaozhou pouring on.

It is sold by year, usually cheaply, and often under other names, so the useful thing to know is how to recognise it: pale wet leaf, honey without much perfume, a finish that stops early. Bought honestly as Bai Ye from a seller who states the garden, it is good value; bought as Wudong Mi Lan Xiang, it is not. For the honeyed style with more depth, go to a true Mi Lan Xiang from the high gardens.
sources_note: The identity of Fenghuang Bai Ye with the Lingtou Dancong cultivar follows Chinese cultivar sources; some Chaozhou sellers treat them as separate strains.
history:
Little that is firmly documented could be found under the name Bai Ye itself. It is a pale-leaved Chaozhou dancong, and it is commonly identified with the plant registered as the national cultivar Lingtou Dancong, the mainstay of tea in Raoping county, where a provincial extension project has promoted it. Some Chaozhou sellers treat the two as separate strains, so that link is the usual view, not a settled fact.

A selection date in the early 1960s circulates for Lingtou Dancong, but no page that could be opened here confirmed it, so it is left out.
